Title: Reading as a Lifeline: Academic Writing Editor's Picks
NewsSummary: Mr Gitonga, a passionate bibliophile, says reading is about making connections

content.text: In the quiet corners of the AKU Kenya's Library, where knowledge and inspiration converge, Augustine Gitonga, the Academic Writing Editor, immerses himself in a world of literature that transcends boundaries. Whether in the stacks of books or the digital archives of research papers, Gitonga's passion for reading goes beyond the act of consumption - it is a journey, a ritual, and an escape.

"I love the way reading cools down my mind," he shares. "When my thoughts are scattered or under pressure, a good book brings me back to focus. It's invigorating; it refreshes my perspective, transports me into new worlds, and equips me with new ideas and ways of thinking. Reading is not just an activity, it's a lifeline."

Gitonga's relationship with books is as dynamic as it is deep. His current read, Fan into Flame: An Autobiography by Kenyan author Reverend Doctor John Gatu, offers a glimpse into his love for works that are both personal and profound. This autobiography gives readers an intimate peek into Gatu's life and struggles, portraying a testimony to resilience and purpose.

Though Gitonga admits he's never been one to revisit a book once he's read it, his selection of books speaks volumes about his intellectual range. "Once I've read a book, it sticks," he explains. However, there is one book that has earned a permanent place close to his heart: Why I Am a Christian by John Stott. It's a book the editor keeps close because of the depth of thought it provides on faith, personal conviction, and spiritual integrity. Gitonga enjoys unfurling the layers of wisdom in this book, and even though he doesn't reread it, he often finds himself revisiting the key concepts.

Gitonga is not just an academic editor; he is a literary enthusiast whose interests span across languages and cultures. His reading is not confined to English; it flows through Swahili and Gikuyu, a Kenyan vernacular language. Kenda Muiyuru: Rũgano rwa Gikũyu na Mumbi by academic and Kenyan award-winning writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o and Siku Njema by former broadcast journalist and Swahili author Ken Walibora are among the works that have had a significant impact on him. Ngũgĩ's Kenda Muiyuru is a powerful retelling of the Gikuyu and Mumbi story - the first man and woman to whom the Agikuyu people trace their origin, and Walibora's works Siku Njema and Ndoto ya Amerika are creative reflections of contemporary African realities. Gitonga regards these books as powerful because they bridge cultural narratives and offer perspectives that might otherwise be lost.

With a sharp eye for both the intellectual and the creative, Mr Gitonga is keen to offer advice to authors, researchers, and anyone passionate about literature. His mantra? Keep writing. "In this age, we are seeing a flourishing of diverse voices and new ideas," he points out. "Authors need to keep writing and engaging with the times. There is so much untapped potential in addressing current issues, challenging societal norms, and venturing into uncharted territories. Books today should aim to inform, educate, and entertain, while being deeply relevant to the moment."

Mr Gitonga also advocates for the accessibility of books, emphasizing the importance of offering both digital and print versions to reach a wider audience. The digital age has changed the way we interact with literature. Authors need to be up- to- date with technology and make their work available in a variety of formats. "At the same time, we must curb the growing issues of plagiarism and piracy, which threaten the integrity of creative work."

For Gitonga, reading isn't just about turning pages; it's about making connections - whether it's the connection between a reader and an author, or the connection between ideas that shape a better world. In his mind, literature has the power to create these links and make the world just a little bit more cohesive. In every word he edits, in every book he reads, Mr Augustine Gitonga reminds us that the journey of knowledge is endless - and, like all great adventures, it's something worth sharing.
